newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori vows to wipe out rebel group.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori vows to wipe out rebel group.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori piled pressure on Marxist rebels holding 73 VIP hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence by warning he aimed to wipe out the group after the crisis.

"This is not going to go unpunished," Fujimori said in La Paz, Bolivia on Thursday. "We are looking for the total eradication of the group in the region," he said, referring to the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).
Speaking to reporters during a brief visit with Bolivia's President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada, Fujimori said he would not let up in his fight against rebel groups in Peru.
"There is no going back. There are still isolated groups ... this government is going to hunt them down," he said.
Fujimori, whose younger brother Pedro is among the captives, has built much of his popular support on an aggressive fight against the MRTA and the larger and bloodier Maoist Shining Path rebel group.
Local analysts say that Fujimori's efforts have reduced the MRTA to less than 250 active members.
Fujimori's threatening tone underlined police tactics over the last few days that have steadily tightened the screws on the defiant MRTA rebels inside the Japanese ambassador's home.

Shortly before dawn on Thursday, four carpenters boarded up one of the compound's two entrances and a small hole in the wall used by service staff. That left open only the entrance used by Red Cross workers, mediators and freed captives.
A police helicopter also flew over the mined and booby-trapped residence several times.
The MRTA responded to the government's latest moves on the Internet, slamming Fujimori as a "dictator" whose security forces were preparing to storm the residence.

In a communique carried on its web home page the MRTA said police activities around the diplomatic compound were "provocations that seek a pretext to justify military intervention ... We ask for the families, the press, human rights organisations and national and international solidarity to help prevent this massacre we warn of."

Continuing the propaganda war from within the residence, the roughly 15 rebels, who are armed with assault rifles and grenade launchers, chanted revolutionary songs and shouted slogans to reporters outside.
"We will carry on until we die. We will not back down in our efforts," they shouted, local Radio Programas del Peru said.

Though both sides have said they are willing to sit down to discuss a peaceful end to the 38-day crisis, Fujimori has ruled out starting talks until the rebels drop their demand for the release of about 400 jailed comrades.
"We are not going to allow (government negotiator Domingo) Palermo to go to the negotiating table unless they accept that there will be no release of prisoners," Fujimori said Wednesday.

In recent days police have driven armoured personnel carriers with heavy machine guns within a few blocks of the residence. Their special force officers have approached the compound's walls, tossed stones into the driveway, peeked around the gate and run backward and forward in a seeming effort to unnerve the MRTA.

Red Cross officials, clearly alarmed by the police maneuvres, said they would cut back their visits to the residence and painted lines on the street outside the compound's entrance on Thursday delimiting an area into which police could not move while they were inside.
The MRTA rebels originally seized hundreds of guests when they stormed a cocktail party at the residence on Dec. 17.

They freed most in what they called "goodwill gestures," keeping those they consider the most important bargaining chips, including two Peruvian ministers, generals, security chiefs, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats and ambassadors from Bolivia and Japan.

The MRTA is holding the Bolivian diplomat in the hope of obtaining the release of four rebels jailed in the neighbouring country. Bolivia has from the outset backed Fujimori's stance on not freeing MRTA prisoners.
